extracted.intended_audience: Readers of The Spectator / polite 18th-century public (educated men and women of fashion); anyone interested in manners, taste, and language
extracted.subtask_description: Short satirical/moral essays (Spectator-style) addressing social conduct, taste, language, and gendered behaviour; mixes anecdote and prescriptive remarks to guide readers' manners and judgments. Useful for composing or evaluating period moralizing satire and advice to polite society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct pronoun usage: who vs which
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons should be referred to with 'who' rather than 'which' (e.g. 'Our Father who art in Heaven' not 'which'). The petition complains of frequent misuse of WHO and WHICH in speech, pulpit and law, and asks for clear assignment of their proper roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples on the page: cites misuses in prayer and Acts of Parliament; notes that learned bodies (convocation) refused an alteration. Anti-pattern: treating persons with 'which' or allowing statutes, prayers, and public speech to habitually substitute 'that' or 'which' for 'who'. The rhetoric implies a normative rule: reserve 'who' for persons and 'which' for things to preserve propriety of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for colloquial expletive 'that' in discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'that' and similar expletive phrases ('that is', 'that is to say', 'such things as that') are defended as necessary for natural discourse and rhetorical length; speakers often need these fillers to continue a tolerable-length discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records a rejoinder from 'THAT' defending its use with many illustrative phrases. Practical guidance: do not rigidly ban common conversational particles that aid discourse; recognize that idiomatic expletives serve communicative functions. Anti-pattern: overly pedantic purism that would eliminate such natural colloquial markers and make speech unnatural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of devotional books: elevate the mind, avoid mechanical religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of devotion chosen for private reading should elevate the mind above worldly concerns and cultivate an inward virtue rather than produce 'mechanical religion'—a set of rote practices disconnected from true morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and warnings: avoid short 'weekly preparations' and texts that prompt a habit of formal prayer as a mere compliment to virtue (e.g., women who spend hours praying yet play cards all day). Recommended: choose authors that encourage true inward piety, temper worldly passions, and produce a real moral improvement rather than affectation. Anti-pattern: devotional reading that is showy, formulaic, or used as an excuse for vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine virtue is inward and habitual, not performative
rubrics_metrics.description: True virtue consists in inward disposition and habits of the mind (e.g., pity for vice accompanying scorn of it), not merely in outward signs, ceremonial acts or the absence of overt wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: characters who keep prayer hours yet behave cruelly at home or devote long hours to cards; 'Dulcianara' who boasts of a moral appearance yet is insolent. Advice: favour moral education that forms habits so virtuous conduct becomes second nature. Anti-pattern: conflating absence of scandalous acts with true virtue or using religious observance as social performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women should prioritize domestic virtues and modesty over partisan public zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are urged to aspire to virtues 'peculiar to your Sex'—natural modesty, tender motherhood, faithful marriage—and to avoid zeal for party politics that leads to public animosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Pericles' funeral oration advising women to 'aspire only to those Virtues that are peculiar to your Sex' and recommends the family as the proper province for private women. Encouraged behaviour: modesty and private service rather than public factionalism. Anti-pattern: women publicly displaying partisan faction (e.g., patches as party-signals) and thereby aggravating national divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partisan signalling and fashionable factionalism (the 'patch' warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public, fashionable signals of party allegiance (exemplified by patches placed on one side of the face to denote Whig or Tory) are criticized as frivolous, divisive, and misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: theatre boxes divided by patch-side; mistaken signalling caused by natural marks (moles, pimples) leading to misrepresentation; some women allegedly stipulate in marriage contracts the right to patch on a chosen side. Advice: resist reducing political allegiance to fashion or face-marking; focus public energy on real common causes. Anti-pattern: adopting party-affiliated dress/ornament that deepens private animosities and confuses personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vanity, rivalry, and competitive displays of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive striving to outshine others in dress and appearance (the Brunetta–Phillis rivalry) leads to mutual hatred, envy, and ruinous behaviour and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative examples: two women whose childhood friendship turns to lifelong enmity over attempts to outdo each other's dress and admirers; schemes to mimic and upstage the rival. Advice: eschew comparison-driven conduct and the artificial costs of maintaining superiority; value dignified behaviour over triumphs of fashion. Anti-pattern: allowing fashion and rivalry to dictate conduct and generate social strife.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship and marriage: don't base decisions solely on appearance or temporary fancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The heart deceives; reliance on sight-only affection leads to unstable choices in lovers. Those who postpone marriage for seasonal pleasures often change their minds many times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From letter of M.T. and commentary: women will 'like ten more before she is fixed' and often accept the worst man they liked. Advice: cultivate love of laudable things and steady judgment rather than being guided merely by sight or fleeting admiration. Anti-pattern: excessive delay to enjoy pleasures that fosters fickle attachments and poor marital choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial prudence and modest household management
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagance after sudden fortune reveals a small mind; one should manage household affairs within a narrow, orderly compass—keep receipts, inventories, and regular oversight to avoid debt and disgrace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: acquaintance who inherited and ran into drunken disputes, broken furniture, and eventual ruin leading to begging. Practical guidance from narrator's own practice: require regular vouchers from estate manager, keep lists of linen and garments with numbers to reconcile with laundress, sign receipts—i.e., orderly accounting. Anti-pattern: ostentatious spending, lack of inventory and oversight, and indulgent company that leads to debt.
